Q: register dependencies versus out of order execution A:

I made the changes you mention, reduces code size a bit, but not measurable change in performance. I'll experiment with align, but with other programs. it wasn't consistent in how it helped on my laptop processor.

For xenc6, the minimum unroll is 6, since the 6 registers are logically cycled in each unrolled loop. For the LFSR shift, instead of shifting data, the registers are logically rotated:

z0<-z5<-z4<-z3<-z2<-z1<-z0<-...

I updated my question to explain this at the end of my question.

This is where the 20% gain in performance occurs, due to avoiding zmm dependencies in the inner loop and using 2 less zmm registers.

For the computed jumps, they would be computed one time and stored as pointers on the stack (to allow multi-threading).

The code is based on 1986|1987 ECC encode converted to use zmm registers.

Q: Programming Language Recommendation for Saas A:

There is no wrong answer to this question. You can find examples of successful SaaS web applications in practically any programming language.

The criterion for choice of programming language is usually for developer productivity instead of deployment cost. You would be better off choosing the language that your developer team is most productive with.

For example, a team of Python developers will be skilled at making a Python app efficient, and thus it will have a low cost of deployment. The same team probably would not have the same skill with code written in, say, Java. So they will work slower, and may not take advantage of best practices of that language. Does this mean Python is better than Java? No, it means that team will get better results using the language with which they have the most expertise.

It's also true that many SaaS services are made up of multiple programming languages. At my last job, the main web service was written in Ruby on Rails. There were also hundreds of microservices backing that web service. Most microservice were written in one of Java, Ruby, or Go. A few were written in Python or Node.js.

Sometimes a given language is more suited for a given task, so you shouldn't limit yourself to one language. And before you can choose the best language for the task, you need to be much more specific about its requirements than you have been in this question.

Q: Why does the finally block execute immediately when calling next() on a generator without assigning it? A:

Because you are not storing a (hard) reference to the generator:

Imediatelly after returning from your next call, the generator created by the get_session_db() call is garbage collected: that will close the generator, and run the finally block inside it. The fact the code in __del__ of the class itself is not executed at this very moment, on the other hand, illustrates why we should not rely on __del__. I don't know which Python mechanism keeps the SessionLocal instance itself from being GCed at the same point .close is called.

Here is what one gets, in a REPL, when the generator returned by the get_session_db() call is kept with a reference (another variable) vs when it doesn't :

Your same snippet - but I put an extra except clause which can show the momment the generator is closed:


class SessionMaker():
    def __init__(self):
        print('Session initiated')
        self.id = id(self)
    def close(self):
        print(f'Close called for Session {self.id}')
    def __del__(self):
        print(f'Session {self.id} finalized (GC)')

# The generator function
def get_session_db():
    session = SessionMaker()
    try:
        yield session
    except BaseException as base:
        print(f"caught {type(base)} exception!")
        raise 
    finally:
        session.close()

Pasting this in the repl and iteracting with it, I get:


In [11]: aa = next(get_session_db())  # no reference kept for the generator!
Session initiated
caught <class 'GeneratorExit'> exception!
Close called for Session 140672511211712

In [12]: bb = get_session_db()  # keep a reference in `bb` 
Session 140672511207680 finalized (GC)  # late finalization of session created in `aa` step: the GC has its own misterous ways: do not rely on `__del__`. 

In [13]: cc = next(bb) # retrieve session instance
Session initiated

In [14]: cc
Out[14]: <__main__.SessionMaker at 0x7ff0df2d5e50>

In [15]: next(bb, "finished")  # Advance generator, closing session
Close called for Session 140672513171024
Out[15]: 'finished'

Moving into your point questions:

In CPython, is it guaranteed that the finally block runs immediately in the session = next(get_session_db()) example?

Yes, if there is no instrumentalization code (debuggers, profiles, loggers, REPL magic code), which could keep a reference to the object returned by get_session_db(), before calling next(...) with it.

However note that the the opposite holds: if you do keep an explicit hard reference to the generator, it won't be arbitrarily closed - and that is not an implementation detail.

Is the current implementation of get_session_db inherently unsafe if the caller does not maintain a reference to the generator object?

Yes.

What is the practical difference of using a Context Manager to prevent premature Garbage Collection in this SQLAlchemy environment?

COntext Managers are a language feature created exactly to help dealing with the edge cases and eventual non-deterministic behavior of garbage collections. So, the practical difference is: using contexg managers will get you covered.

FOr one thing: let's suppose you re-write your code to rely on the lack-of-reference implying that the generator is collected after the next call: Python's concurrency efforts already in effect in 3.14, like the "free threading" runtime change the behavior of the garbage collector, so that this is not deterministic any more, even for an official, PSF blessed, cPython build.

Even if contextlib.contextmanager implements context managers around generators, it is MEANT to keep consistency across implementation details - with a lot of edge case, and internal details consideration, all of which one would have to account for in the case above.
